region: Uzbekistan (Tashkent, Samarkand, Bukhara, Khiva and the Khorezm fortresses), a day across the border at Penjikent in Tajikistan, and south-east Kazakhstan (Almaty, Medeu and Charyn Canyon)
title: Central Asia — Tiled Cities and Desert Fortresses of the Silk Road
subtitle: Two weeks by high-speed train, hired car and yurt camp, from Samarkand's madrasas to the red canyons of Kazakhstan
summary: A 14-day Silk Road circuit through Uzbekistan's four great cities and the ancient Khorezm desert fortresses, with a day in Tajik Penjikent and a finish in Almaty and Charyn Canyon. Winter-compatible by design: city and rail based, no high mountain passes.
introduction: You land in Tashkent, spend a morning in the domed Chorsu bazaar and take the Afrosiyob high-speed train to Samarkand, where the Registan, Gur-e Amir and the tiled lane of Shah-i-Zinda fill two days. A day trip crosses the Zarafshan valley into Tajikistan to the 5,000-year-old settlement of Sarazm and the Sogdian town of Penjikent. Then Bukhara's brick minarets and tea houses, a long drive across the Kyzylkum desert to walled Khiva on Navruz, and a night in a heated yurt beside the mud-brick fortresses of ancient Khorezm. Two flights bring you to Almaty for the snowy Trans-Ili Alatau and the red-rock Valley of Castles at Charyn Canyon.

exceptional.vsOman: Oman is a self-drive, tent-and-4x4 trip across empty landscape. This one is the reverse: dense living cities, fast trains, hired drivers and the world's best tiled architecture, with desert and canyon as a counterpoint in the last third. The camping is limited to a single heated yurt night because March nights fall below freezing.
exceptional.vsPackageTourism: Standard Silk Road packages move groups through Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva by coach in a few days. This plan uses scheduled trains and shared local transport, stays in family guesthouses in the old towns, adds a border-crossing day in Tajikistan and the Khorezm fortresses that most packages skip, and ends in a second country with a different landscape.
exceptional.vsPortfolio: No other destination in the portfolio combines three UNESCO-listed Timurid and Islamic cities with Soviet-era Almaty, a Tajik day trip, Navruz celebrations in Khiva and a 21st-century high-speed rail network, all by public transport and in winter-to-spring conditions without technical terrain.

coordinates.label: Uzbekistan Silk Road cities and south-east Kazakhstan

duration.note: Day 1 is the outbound flight (arrival early on day 2); day 14 is the return flight from Almaty. Day 11 includes two domestic or regional flights.

recommendedTravelWindow.rationale: Ramadan 2027 ends around 9 March, so the whole window is after it; Navruz (21 March) falls on day 9 in Khiva; Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva reach 13–16 °C by day; the snow in Almaty and at Charyn Canyon has largely retreated from the valleys. Mid-February is 5–8 degrees colder, often snowy and falls entirely inside Ramadan.

februarySuitability.summary: Cold but dry enough in the cities (Samarkand about 9 °C by day, around 0 °C at night, snow on average on 7 days); Almaty is genuinely wintry (2.7 °C mean maximum, −6 °C mean minimum, 13 snowy days). Ramadan runs for the entire month, which affects daytime restaurants and ticket-hall hours. Sites are quiet and cheap. Yurt camping in the desert is unpleasant.

marchSuitability.summary: Samarkand averages about 15 °C by day and 5 °C at night, Almaty about 10 °C and 0 °C; the desert around Khiva is cool but workable. March is the wettest month in Samarkand (about 73 mm), so expect some rain days. Navruz on 21 March brings public festivals and also heavy domestic travel on trains and in hotels.

climate.regionNote: Figures are 1991–2020-style climate normals for Samarkand (Uzbek cities; Bukhara and Khiva are drier and a degree or two warmer by day) and Almaty (Kazakhstan). No 2027 forecast exists; treat as planning ranges. The Wikipedia climate tables were read on 2026-11-28.

february.rainfall: Samarkand about 52 mm over the month with snow on about 7 days; Almaty about 43 mm with snow on about 13 days; Khiva and Bukhara are dry (below 20 mm).
february.humidity: Moderate to high in the cities in winter; fog is common
february.notes: Almaty mean daily maximum 2.7 °C, minimum −6.2 °C; Samarkand 9.5 °C and −0.2 °C. Desert nights at Khiva typically fall below −5 °C in February.

march.rainfall: Samarkand about 73 mm (the wettest month) with snow on about 3 days; Almaty about 72 mm with snow on about 8 days; Bukhara and Khiva 20–30 mm.
march.notes: Samarkand mean daily maximum 15.2 °C and minimum 4.6 °C; Almaty 9.9 °C and −0.2 °C. Nights in the Khorezm desert are still around 0 °C.

climate.snowAndMountainAccess: The Fann Mountains and Iskanderkul in Tajikistan and the Pamir Highway are snowbound in February and March and are not part of this route (winter closures are standard; unsuitable without winter-expedition logistics). The route stays in lowlands and city bases. In Kazakhstan, Medeu and Shymbulak (about 1,700–2,300 m) are snow-covered and open; the Big Almaty Lake road and the Kolsai Lakes are winter-limited and the Kolsai area lies in a border zone that may need a permit, so neither is planned.
climate.seaConditions: Not relevant: no coast on the route.
climate.airQuality: Winter air pollution is significant in Tashkent and the Fergana Valley (FCDO notes poor air quality from November to February) and in Almaty on still winter days; March is better. Consider a mask for sensitive travellers.
climate.wildlifeSeasonality: Not a wildlife trip. Spring migration begins in March around the Aral Sea; saiga and Przewalski's horse are not on the route.

holidaysAndFestivals.name: Ramadan
holidaysAndFestivals.impact: Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan are secular and most tourist restaurants stay open, but local-only restaurants may close at lunchtime in smaller towns; the window 13–26 March avoids it.

holidaysAndFestivals.name: Eid al-Fitr
holidaysAndFestivals.impact: Public holiday; domestic travel peaks just before the proposed window.

holidaysAndFestivals.name: Navruz (Persian new year, spring equinox)
holidaysAndFestivals.dates: 21 March 2027 (public holidays expected around 20–22 March in Uzbekistan and 21–23 March in Kazakhstan; not verified)
holidaysAndFestivals.impact: Street festivals, sumalak (wheat-germ pudding) cooked overnight and folk performances in Khiva on day 9. Trains and guesthouses fill up; book Afrosiyob tickets and rooms early. FCDO notes a 2024 plot against Nowruz events in Tajikistan, so avoid large crowds in Tajikistan on this date.

climate.ramadan2027: Ramadan is about 8 February – 9 March 2027. A mid- to late-March window avoids it entirely. In February it would run throughout the trip.
climate.lunarNewYear2027: Not relevant: 6 February 2027 has no effect on Uzbekistan or Kazakhstan.
climate.tourismDemand: Low in February; moderate in March, with a peak around Navruz and the April–May and September–October high seasons still to come. Heritage sites are uncrowded.
climate.flightPriceSeasonality: Winter fares to Tashkent are the lowest of the year; Navruz and Eid weeks push regional fares up. Not verified against live data.

geography.summary: A 3,000 km arc from the Zarafshan oasis cities, through the Kyzylkum and Khorezm desert along the Amu Darya delta, to the Trans-Ili Alatau range and the Charyn river canyon in south-east Kazakhstan.
geography.distinctive: Oasis cities on irrigated river valleys separated by true desert; a 150 km red sandstone canyon (Charyn) that is a Kazakh equivalent of the American south-west; and ancient fortresses scattered across the Khorezm plain.

landscapes.name: Zarafshan valley and Kyzylkum
landscapes.description: Samarkand and Bukhara sit on an irrigated river plain; the road from Bukhara to Khiva crosses about 450 km of the Kyzylkum desert.

landscapes.name: Khorezm fortresses
landscapes.description: Toprak-Kala and Ayaz-Kala are mud-brick fortresses in desert flats near the Amu Darya delta, many from the 1st–7th centuries.

landscapes.name: Charyn Canyon, Valley of Castles
landscapes.description: A 154 km river canyon with 150–300 m eroded sandstone walls, about 200 km east of Almaty.

landscapes.name: Trans-Ili Alatau above Almaty
landscapes.description: Snow-covered range reaching 4,600 m directly behind the city; Medeu at 1,700 m and Shymbulak at 2,200 m are an hour from the centre.

culture.summary: Timurid and Islamic architecture at its peak, living bazaars, family guesthouses, Sogdian and Khorezmian archaeology, and Navruz. Kazakhstan adds Soviet and nomadic heritage.

culturalHighlights.name: Registan, Gur-e Amir and Shah-i-Zinda, Samarkand
culturalHighlights.description: Three madrasas of the 15th–17th centuries, Timur's tomb with its ribbed dome, and a lane of 14th–15th century mausoleums covered in glazed tile. Hire a local guide for one half-day.

culturalHighlights.name: Bukhara old city
culturalHighlights.description: The Kalon Minaret (1127), the Ark fortress, the Samanid mausoleum (10th century) and the trading domes. Evening at the Lyab-i Hauz pool among tea houses. About 140 monuments in a walkable core.

culturalHighlights.name: Khiva Itchan Kala and Navruz
culturalHighlights.description: A mud-brick walled inner town of mosques, madrasas and minarets, entered by four gates. On 21 March the town hosts Navruz celebrations: sumalak, music and folk games.

culturalHighlights.name: Sarazm and Penjikent, Tajikistan
culturalHighlights.description: Sarazm is a 4th–3rd millennium BCE proto-urban settlement on the UNESCO list; Penjikent has the ruins of a Sogdian town with 5th–8th century wall paintings, now in the Hermitage and in the local museum.

culturalHighlights.name: Khorezm fortresses
culturalHighlights.description: Toprak-Kala, a palace of the Kushan period, and Ayaz-Kala, a hilltop fortress. Walkable and almost empty in winter. A hired driver is needed.

culturalHighlights.name: Chorsu and Siab bazaars
culturalHighlights.description: Daily markets for bread, dried fruit, spices, plov and manti. Eating where locals eat is part of the plan on days 2 and 4.

culturalHighlights.name: Almaty
culturalHighlights.description: A Soviet-planned and now contemporary city: Zenkov Cathedral (a wooden Orthodox church), the Green Bazaar, Kok-Tobe viewpoint and the Medeu ice rink.

adventureHighlights.name: Charyn Canyon Valley of Castles walk
adventureHighlights.description: A 2–3 hour walk descending 150 m to the river inside the canyon; in March the path can be icy at the top.

adventureHighlights.name: Medeu and Shymbulak winter mountain day
adventureHighlights.description: Cable car and gondola from Medeu (1,700 m) to Shymbulak (2,200 m) and a winter walk; skis and boots can be hired. Not a technical mountain objective.

adventureHighlights.name: Desert fortress circuit and yurt night
adventureHighlights.description: A day of walking among Khorezm fortresses, then a night in a heated yurt camp near Ayaz-Kala. Check that the camp is open in March; some close from November to March.

adventureHighlights.name: Overland border crossing to Tajikistan
adventureHighlights.description: Cross the Samarkand–Penjikent border on foot between shared taxis. An e-visa and a check of whether the crossing is open to foreigners are essential.

signatureExperiences.title: Dawn at the Registan and the tile lanes of Samarkand
signatureExperiences.description: Two days on foot at Samarkand's monuments, timed for early light at the Registan and Shah-i-Zinda, with a local guide for one half-day to read the tilework and history.
signatureExperiences.whyDistinctive: Far fewer visitors in March than in high season, and the tile and calligraphy detail rewards slow looking.
signatureExperiences.howToOrganise: Buy tickets at each site; a licensed guide for a half-day about €40 for the group; stay in a guesthouse within walking distance of the Registan.
signatureExperiences.costNote: Entrance tickets for the three main sites about €18–25 per person (estimate; ticket prices rise regularly).

signatureExperiences.title: Navruz in Khiva's walled town
signatureExperiences.description: Spend 21 March inside Itchan Kala for the spring-equinox festival, eating sumalak and watching folk performances, then walk the walls at dusk.
signatureExperiences.whyDistinctive: One of the few places in the world where a UNESCO walled city hosts a Navruz celebration inside its ramparts.
signatureExperiences.howToOrganise: Book a guesthouse inside or beside the walls well in advance; the combined Itchan Kala ticket is about €10 (estimate).
signatureExperiences.costNote: Itchan Kala ticket estimate; festival access normally free.

signatureExperiences.title: Khorezm fortresses and a night in a heated yurt
signatureExperiences.description: A hired driver takes the group across the Amu Darya delta to Toprak-Kala and Ayaz-Kala, followed by a night in a yurt camp with a stove and a Khorezmian dinner.
signatureExperiences.whyDistinctive: The only remote-night experience on the route: desert silence and stars, with 2,000-year-old brick walls at your door.
signatureExperiences.howToOrganise: Arrange the driver and a yurt camp through a Khiva guesthouse. Confirm in advance that the camp is open and heated in March.
signatureExperiences.costNote: Driver share about €25 plus yurt camp with dinner about €40 and site tickets (estimate, unconfirmed).

signatureExperiences.title: Charyn Canyon's Valley of Castles
signatureExperiences.description: A hired car from Almaty to the Charyn river canyon, a walk down to the river between 200 m red rock towers, and lunch at a roadside cafe.
signatureExperiences.whyDistinctive: Kazakhstan's red-rock canyon in March, uncrowded, with snow on the rim and an hour of light that photographers seek.
signatureExperiences.howToOrganise: A driver for the day (about €110–150 for the car, shared by four); entrance to the park is a few euros per person; allow 3–3.5 h each way.
signatureExperiences.costNote: Car with driver share plus entrance, estimate.

travelStyle.summary: City-based by high-speed and scheduled trains, with hired drivers for desert and canyon days, two short flights between Khiva and Almaty, and one yurt night.

transport.summary: Uzbekistan's Afrosiyob high-speed trains link Tashkent, Samarkand and Bukhara (about 2 h and 1.5 h on the legs used here). The 450 km road from Bukhara to Khiva crosses desert in 6–7 h; the alternative is a slower train to Urgench. Two flights (Urgench–Tashkent, Tashkent–Almaty) cover the long gap to Kazakhstan. City taxis use ride-hailing apps.

modes.description: Tashkent–Samarkand on day 3 and Samarkand–Bukhara on day 6; book via the operator's website or at the station; seats fill around Navruz.
Bukhara–Khiva (day 8), Khorezm fortresses (day 10), Samarkand–Penjikent border (day 5), Almaty–Charyn (day 13). Agree the price before starting and ask the guesthouse for a reliable driver.
Urgench–Tashkent and Tashkent–Almaty on day 11; carriers include Uzbekistan Airways and Air Astana (not verified for the date).
Ride-hailing apps are common in Tashkent and Almaty; the Tashkent metro is cheap and photogenic.

transport.carRental: Not recommended: unfamiliar road conditions, police checkpoints, border and registration formalities, and winter weather. Hired cars with drivers are inexpensive and are assumed in the budget.

drivingRequirements.summary: Self-drive is not planned. Roads between the cities are generally paved but driver standards vary, police checks are frequent, and cross-border rental is complicated; hired drivers cost little.
drivingRequirements.internationalDrivingPermit: An International Driving Permit (1949 or 1968 Convention) is normally required alongside a national licence for foreign drivers in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan; not needed on this plan. Verify per licence country before booking any self-drive.
drivingRequirements.licenceNotes: Two of the four travellers hold car licences; the plan needs no licensed driver. The other two travellers are not affected.
drivingRequirements.motorcycleNotes: No motorcycles or scooters on this plan. Alternatives used: high-speed train, shared taxi, hired driver, metro.
drivingRequirements.recommendedApproach: Trains for the Tashkent–Samarkand–Bukhara corridor, hired drivers with fixed prices for desert and canyon days, flights for the long Khiva–Almaty gap.

accommodation.summary: Family-run guesthouses and boutique hotels in converted old houses in Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva (typically US$30–60 for a twin room including breakfast), a hotel in Tashkent, a mid-range hotel in Almaty and one heated yurt camp.

camping.summary: Tent camping is not recommended in March: night temperatures at or below 0 °C and registration rules (FCDO notes campers must register themselves on the Emehmon system, which requires an Uzbek card). The plan uses one night in a heated yurt camp. Camps may be closed in winter; this must be confirmed by message before booking.

physicalDifficulty.label: moderate
physicalDifficulty.summary: Mostly walking in cities and low-intensity hikes. The hardest days are the 6–7 h Bukhara–Khiva drive, day 11 with two flights, and the Charyn canyon walk (about 300 m of climb on the way back). Cold winds are the main discomfort.

itinerary.summary: Fly into Tashkent, take trains to Samarkand and Bukhara, cross by road to Tajikistan for one day, drive across the Kyzylkum to Khiva for Navruz and a yurt night, fly to Almaty and finish at Charyn Canyon. About 3,000 km of surface and air travel, but only three long driving days (Bukhara–Khiva, Khorezm, Charyn). Two flexible days (5 and 13) absorb weather and border problems.

Option B (no Tajik visa, bad weather or crossing closed): Shahrisabz, Timur's birthplace, 90 km south over the Tashtakaracha pass
Return to Samarkand by evening

Evening cooking class or tea-house dinner

Juma Mosque with its forest of carved wooden columns
Navruz festival: sumalak, music and folk games
Sunset from a rooftop terrace

Flights are an open-jaw Paris–Tashkent and Almaty–Paris estimate, included in every headline total.
Navruz (21 March) may raise hotel and train prices; the realistic scenario carries a 12% contingency.
Cash economy: ATMs work in cities and cards in better hotels, but payments in guesthouses are often cash.

scenarioNotes.economical: Hostel-grade guesthouses, economy train seats, no Tajik day, fewer guides, hand-baggage only.
scenarioNotes.realistic: Guesthouses and mid-range old-town hotels, Afrosiyob economy, hired cars for the desert and canyon days, three guided half-days and the Tajik day trip.
scenarioNotes.comfortable: Boutique hotels, business-class trains, a private driver for most days, five guided days.

security.summary: On the assessed route (Uzbekistan's Tashkent–Samarkand–Bukhara–Khiva corridor, one day trip to Penjikent in Tajikistan, and Almaty–Charyn in Kazakhstan) no official source advises against all or all-but-essential travel. The route avoids the Afghan border zones, Termez, GBAO, Khatlon, the Tajik–Kyrgyz border and the Kazakh restricted border strips. Terrorism and border-security notes for Tajikistan keep the Penjikent day optional and re-checkable.
security.assessedRoute: Tashkent, Samarkand, Penjikent and Sarazm (Tajikistan, 45 km from Samarkand), Bukhara, Khiva and the Toprak-Kala/Ayaz-Kala area in Khorezm, then Almaty, Medeu and Charyn Canyon. Excludes Termez and the Afghan border, Karakalpakstan interior, Dushanbe and southern Tajikistan, GBAO, the Fann Mountains and Pamir roads, and Kolsai.

advisories.level: Border zone with Afghanistan formally advised against; rest of the country heightened vigilance. Page updated 15 September 2026; zone map updated 11 March 2026.
advisories.routeImpact: Route does not enter Termez or the border zone.

advisories.routeImpact: Penjikent is in the north-west, about 250 km from the Afghan border; stay on roads.

advisories.routeImpact: Almaty and Charyn are outside restricted areas.

advisories.regionsAffected: Afghan border, Tajik–Kyrgyz border, GBAO, Tavildara
advisories.routeImpact: None of these areas are on the route.

advisories.level: Uzbekistan Level 1; Kazakhstan Level 1; Tajikistan Level 2 (reconsider travel to the Afghan border and GBAO).
Yellow for Tajikistan, Kazakhstan and most of Uzbekistan; Orange for Termez and the 5 km Afghan border strip in Uzbekistan.
advisories.regionsAffected: Termez and the 5 km Afghan border strip

conflictRisk.note: No active conflict on the route. Armed clashes and incursions are reported along the Tajik–Afghan border and (2021–2025) the Tajik–Kyrgyz border, both far from the planned places; rockets were fired from Afghanistan into southern Uzbekistan in 2022.

terrorismRisk.note: FCDO says attacks in Uzbekistan cannot be ruled out and that terrorists are likely to try to attack in Tajikistan, including during Nowruz; ISKP has claimed attacks on the Tajik–Afghan border (2018–2019, and attacks on Chinese workers in 2025). France rates the Kazakh threat to French nationals as low but not excluded.

kidnappingRisk.note: No kidnapping warning for the planned regions in the sources read.

regionalRestrictions: Do not approach the Afghan border, the Termez region or the fenced Amu Darya border strip.
Foreigners need a permit for border strips (25 km along external borders) in Kazakhstan; Kolsai Lakes are not planned.
GBAO and the Pamir require a separate Tajik permit and are not planned.
Stay on roads near the Uzbek–Tajik border: unmarked mines.
Tajik crossings can close without notice; verify before leaving Samarkand.
ordinaryRisks: Pickpocketing and bag-snatching in bazaars and on trains.
Traffic: poor driver discipline and winter road conditions; use hired drivers with a clean record.
Ice at the Charyn canyon rim and on the Medeu paths.
Winter air pollution in Tashkent and Almaty.
Photography restrictions near government and security sites; carry the passport at all times.
Earthquakes in the south-east of Kazakhstan (Dutch advice).
security.medicalAccess: Good private clinics in Tashkent and Almaty; poor and basic elsewhere (FCDO describes Uzbek healthcare as generally poor). Medical evacuation insurance is essential, especially for the Tajik day trip.
security.insuranceConsiderations: Choose a policy that explicitly covers Tajikistan and does not exclude political violence; some insurers treat the Tajik–Afghan border region as excluded. Check if day trips on foot across a border are covered.
security.reassessmentRequired: Re-check all advisories before booking and two weeks before departure. Triggers: any change in French, UK or Dutch advice for Samarkand or Penjikent; new clashes or incursions in Tajikistan away from the Afghan border; any incident in Uzbekistan or Kazakhstan involving foreigners; closure of the Samarkand–Penjikent crossing. If any trigger occurs, drop day 5 option A (Shahrisabz is the fallback) and re-classify.

practicalRequirements.visa: Depends entirely on passports. FCDO says British citizens can visit Uzbekistan for up to 30 days without a visa and Kazakhstan for up to 30 days visa-free (with a free QazETA recommended now and mandatory from 1 July 2027). Tajikistan needs an e-visa (allow at least two weeks). EU citizens must check each embassy; no nationality is assumed.
practicalRequirements.entry: Uzbekistan: register with local authorities within 3 days (hotels usually do this); declare currency over US$10,000; drones prohibited. Kazakhstan: hotels register arrivals within 3 working days. Tajikistan: crossing by land at Penjikent should be checked in advance.
practicalRequirements.passportValidity: Uzbekistan 3 months after arrival; Kazakhstan 30 days after arrival; Tajikistan 6 months and 2 blank pages (British advice).
permits: No permits needed on the route; a border-zone permit would be required for the Kolsai Lakes and the Chinese border strips, which are not planned.
GBAO permit is needed only for the Pamir, which is excluded.
practicalRequirements.insurance: Travel and medical insurance with evacuation, valid for Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Kazakhstan.
practicalRequirements.connectivity: Local eSIMs or SIM cards work in the cities (passport needed to buy). Coverage is good on the rail corridor and weak in the desert.
practicalRequirements.payments: Cash (soums, tenge) and cards in cities; ATMs in Tashkent, Samarkand, Bukhara and Almaty; carry clean euro or US dollar notes as a backup. Cash is needed in guesthouses, bazaars and for hired drivers.
practicalRequirements.medical: Standard vaccines; check TravelHealthPro. Altitude sickness is not a concern at Medeu.
equipment: Warm layers, windproof jacket, hat and gloves
Sturdy walking boots with grip for icy paths
Sleeping-bag liner for the yurt night
Copy of passport and registration slips

advantages: Famous Silk Road cities with few visitors in March, cheap rail and drivers.
Winter-compatible by design: no high passes, a heated yurt instead of a tent.
Navruz falls inside the trip, inside Khiva's walls.
Three landscapes in two weeks: oasis cities, desert fortresses, canyon and snow range.
Most of the trip is by rail and public transport: no driver licences needed.
disadvantages: Cold nights and variable weather: March is the wettest month in Samarkand and Almaty still sees snow.
Camping is effectively replaced by a single yurt night, so this is less remote than the Oman benchmark.
Tajik day trip depends on an e-visa and border conditions; Fann Mountains and the Pamir are out of season.
Heritage ticket prices for foreigners have risen; Navruz raises hotel prices and fills trains.
Winter air pollution in Tashkent and Almaty.
uncertainties: Open-jaw flight prices to Tashkent and from Almaty are a planning estimate; none was seen live.
Whether the Samarkand–Penjikent crossing is open to foreign tourists and how long formalities take in March 2027.
Whether yurt camps near Ayaz-Kala are open and heated in March; and Navruz holiday dates and prices for 2027.
Uzbek tourist ticket and hotel prices in soums are volatile; euro equivalents are approximate.
